title: Establishing psychological wellbeing metrics for the built environment
central_proposition: An innovative wellbeing valuation approach, combining a multi-item psychological wellbeing scale and Social Return on Investment (SROI) techniques, can produce transferable, monetised metrics to quantify and communicate the value of design in the built environment.

concept_definitions.name: Wellbeing
concept_definitions.definition: A combination of thinking, feeling, and functioning, defined as cognitive satisfaction (achieved through goal accomplishment), the presence of positive affect (and lack of negative feelings), in combination with the psychological needs of competence (personal ability), relatedness (social ties), and autonomy (personal control and resilience). This is represented by the SACRA model (Satisfaction, Affect, Competence, Relatedness, Autonomy).

concept_definitions.name: Wellbeing Valuation
concept_definitions.definition: An approach consisting of a multi-item scale to measure and quantify wellbeing outcomes experienced by building users, and impact reporting techniques using Social Return on Investment (SROI) to produce transferable, monetised evaluation metrics.

concept_definitions.name: SACRA model
concept_definitions.definition: A psychological wellbeing model comprising five components: Satisfaction, Affect, Competence, Relatedness, and Autonomy, derived from self-determination theory and existing wellbeing scales.

concept_definitions.name: Social Return on Investment (SROI)
concept_definitions.definition: A methodology designed to measure and account for a wider concept of value, based on traditional cost-benefit analysis, that assigns a monetary value to social returns using financial proxies to produce an SROI ratio of costs to social outcomes.

argument_structure: The paper first identifies a gap in current built environment evaluation: a lack of robust, psychologically-informed, and monetized metrics for wellbeing. It then proposes a novel wellbeing valuation approach, detailing its two main components: a multi-item psychological wellbeing scale (Building Wellbeing scale) based on the SACRA model, and the application of Social Return on Investment (SROI) methodology to monetize the scale's outcomes. The argument concludes by highlighting how this integrated approach can create a powerful business case for user-centred design and foster new knowledge.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The proposed mechanism involves built environment features influencing the psychological needs and states of building users (as defined by the SACRA model). These psychological outcomes are then quantified using the Building Wellbeing scale. Subsequently, the SROI methodology translates these quantitative wellbeing scores into monetary values using financial proxies, thereby demonstrating the economic 'return' of design on human wellbeing. This monetized value is intended to serve as a clear, transferable metric for decision-making.

findings.mechanism: Increasing demand necessitates evidence-based design proven to deliver these outcomes.
findings.quote: Increasing demand for user-centred environments means evidence-based design proven to deliver wellbeing outcomes for end users is essential.

findings.consequent: Increase in productivity or performance of building users
findings.mechanism: New definitions and methods are required to effectively establish this link, as existing frameworks do not explicitly prove this relationship.
findings.quote: Further, being able to make the link between increased wellbeing and an increase in the productivity, or performance, of building users requires new definitions and methods.

findings.consequent: Communication of the value of design
findings.mechanism: This combination produces transferable, monetised evaluation metrics, enhancing the power and accessibility of design value communication.
findings.quote: This combination has the capability to communicate the value of design in a powerful and accessible manner.

findings.consequent: Development of new user-driven knowledge and shaping the built environment
findings.mechanism: These metrics represent an opportunity to generate new knowledge and guide built environment development.
findings.quote: Wellbeing valuation metrics represent an opportunity to develop new user-driven knowledge and shape the built environment in positive ways.

findings.antecedent: Wellbeing (defined as thinking, feeling, functioning, cognitive satisfaction, positive affect, competence, relatedness, autonomy - SACRA model)
findings.mechanism: The synthesis of cognition and emotion with effective function (flourishing) is crucial for making the business case for increased wellbeing outcomes leading to performance gains.
findings.quote: The synthesis of cognition and emotion with effective function, equating to the concept of flourishing, is of particular importance in the context of growing demands to make the case for increased wellbeing outcomes leading to increases in occupant performance.

findings.antecedent: Built environment (physical design features, environmental conditions, organisational culture, individual practices)
findings.mechanism: There is a current lack of evidence-based research investigating these influences, necessitating a wider, psychologically-informed definition and measurement approach.
findings.quote: As a result, there is a lack of evidence-based research that investigates the ways that the built environment can influence wellbeing outcomes, and particularly when defined in terms of individual flourishing.

findings.antecedent: Building Wellbeing scale (multi-item scale based on SACRA)
findings.consequent: Quantification of wellbeing outcomes for end users
findings.mechanism: It provides a simple, accessible, and cost-effective method to produce a range of wellbeing data and metrics, including individual scores, overall building scores, and SACRA component scores.
findings.quote: The Building Wellbeing scale represents a simple, accessible and cost effective method to quantify the wellbeing outcomes experienced by the end users of a built environment.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The scale has been piloted in a series of case building typologies, including commercial offices, non-clinical healthcare centres, university libraries and student residential halls during 2016 and 2017, with more than 2,000 responses collected overall.

findings.antecedent: Monetisation of quantitative wellbeing scores using SROI
findings.mechanism: Assigning a monetary value to wellbeing outcomes makes them comparable to typical post-occupancy evaluation summaries and facilitates dissemination within the design and construction industry.
findings.quote: Assigning a monetary value to wellbeing outcomes is anticipated to enhance transferability compared to typical post-occupancy evaluation summaries, facilitating the dissemination and implementation of findings within the design and construction industry.

findings.consequent: Representation of return generated by the building for users
findings.mechanism: The SROI methodology compares monetized social returns (wellbeing outcomes) against investment (building costs) using financial proxies.
findings.quote: The SROI ratio represents the return generated by the building for the building users in a year, per every £1 spent.

findings.consequent: More objective information about building impact on end user wellbeing
findings.mechanism: Its basis in a psychological definition of wellbeing allows for a firmer link between wellbeing and performance, moving beyond anecdotal evidence.
findings.quote: The resulting metrics will inform interested parties about the impact of a building, or different spaces within a building, on end user wellbeing in a more objective manner than relying on anecdotal evidence.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The Building Wellbeing scale will accurately measure the five components of psychological wellbeing (Satisfaction, Affect, Competence, Relatedness, Autonomy) in building users.
The monetized wellbeing metrics derived from the SROI methodology will effectively communicate the value of design in financial terms to stakeholders.
The application of the wellbeing valuation approach will facilitate the identification of specific built environment features that influence user wellbeing and performance.
The proposed approach will enable a clearer link between increased user wellbeing and improved performance in built environments.
bridge_warrants: Connects psychological wellbeing (self-determination theory, flourishing, hedonic/eudaimonic wellbeing) to built environment evaluation.
Connects quantitative psychological measurement (WEMWBS, QEWB) to a new context (built environment).
Connects social impact measurement (SROI) to the built environment sector for financial valuation.
Connects wellbeing outcomes to economic value, establishing a 'business case' for design.
methodological_critiques: Existing wellbeing definitions in the built environment are often narrow, typically synonymous with health, comfort, or happiness, lacking a clear, comprehensive definition.
There is a lack of systematic, academically-informed design guidelines to promote buildings that generate wellbeing outcomes.
Only a small number of approaches and tools exist for measuring wellbeing outcomes in the built environment, with no direct measure beyond self-report questions.
Academic work on measuring wellbeing tends to be split between cognitive (long-term satisfaction) and affective (short-term emotions).
Research typically focuses on preventing health or comfort-related problems rather than considering the potential psychological benefits of positive stimuli.
There is a lack of evidence-based research investigating how the built environment influences wellbeing outcomes, particularly when defined as individual flourishing.
Existing frameworks for evaluation do not explicitly prove the relationship between increased wellbeing and improved occupant performance, nor generate learning about how to achieve it in practice.
There is a lack of robust wellbeing measures applicable in post-occupancy evaluations of buildings.
model_structure: The proposed wellbeing valuation approach integrates a psychologically-informed definition of wellbeing (flourishing, operationalized by the SACRA model: Satisfaction, Affect, Competence, Relatedness, Autonomy) with a multi-item measurement scale (Building Wellbeing scale) and a financial reporting methodology (Social Return on Investment - SROI) to produce monetized, transferable metrics.
limitations: The wellbeing valuation approach presented is still under development.
The inherent subjectivity of the SROI valuation process requires full transparency.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The business case for wellbeing is now an influential agenda in the built environment. Increasing demand for user-centred environments means evidence-based design proven to deliver wellbeing outcomes for end users is essential. The challenge is to effectively capture and disseminate this evidence to a range of expert and non-expert audiences. Further, being able to make the link between increased wellbeing and an increase in the productivity, or performance, of building users requires new definitions and methods. An innovative wellbeing valuation approach is presented, consisting of a multi-item scale to measure and quantify the wellbeing outcomes experienced by building users, and impact reporting techniques using Social Return on Investment to produce transferable, monetised evaluation metrics. This combination has the capability to communicate the value of design in a powerful and accessible manner. Wellbeing valuation metrics represent an opportunity to develop new user-driven knowledge and shape the built environment in positive ways.  Practical application: Wellbeing has become an influential agenda in the built environment in recent years, suggesting that user-centred priorities will become increasingly significant to the design and construction sector. The wellbeing valuation approach presented represents an innovative blend of a psychological wellbeing model, quantitative measurement and financial reporting to produce transferable metrics to communicate the value of design in a powerful and transformative manner. Wellbeing valuation is a nascent practice, but it provides the professions with opportunities to collaborate with end users and develop new knowledge about buildings, enhancing the ability of practitioners to shape the built environment in positive ways.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The characteristics and design of the built environment significantly influence human psychological states and overall wellbeing.
Psychological wellbeing is a complex, multi-faceted construct encompassing various dimensions such as emotional, cognitive, social, and physical aspects.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Integrated Framework for Built Environment Wellbeing
theory_commitments.specific_claim: A comprehensive and integrated framework is necessary to systematically assess the impact of specific built environment features on multi-dimensional psychological wellbeing outcomes.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes that built environment features influence psychological wellbeing through mediating perceptual, cognitive, and affective processes, leading to improved wellbeing outcomes for end users.

steps.from_construct: Built environment features (e.g., spatial layout, aesthetics, access to nature, user-centred design elements)
steps.to_construct: Perceived environmental qualities (e.g., spaciousness, beauty, restorativeness, sense of control)
Cognitive and affective responses (e.g., reduced stress, increased positive mood, enhanced cognitive function, sense of autonomy)
Overall psychological wellbeing (e.g., emotional stability, personal growth, social integration)

instruments_used.name: Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire used to measure current positive and negative emotional states, proposed as a metric for emotional wellbeing.

instruments_used.name: Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS)
instruments_used.description: A 5-item self-report scale assessing an individual's global cognitive judgment of their life satisfaction, proposed as a metric for cognitive wellbeing.

instruments_used.name: Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS)
instruments_used.description: A 14-item scale designed to measure mental wellbeing, including aspects of positive affect and psychological functioning, proposed as a comprehensive wellbeing metric.
